name: fix
rationale: The general-purpose starting point for any small change. It front-loads understanding and discovery of the project's own test commands, keeps the change minimal, and makes "ran the tests" part of the definition of done, which is what reviewers check first.
feedback:
New feedback on {{issue.id}} (branch {{branch}}, PR/MR: {{pr.url}}):

{{feedback}}

Handle every item:
- Change request: make the change, or explain why you think it should not be made.
- Question: answer it. Change code only if the answer shows something is wrong.
- Review comment on a file and line: read that code as it is now first; it may have moved.
- No action needed: acknowledge briefly.
If items contradict each other, or one needs a decision only a human can make, ask with request_input instead of choosing.
After changes, run the relevant tests again and commit.
In your final answer, reply to each item by its number, for example "[2] Renamed as suggested.", then a line with only --- and how you verified the changes. Use the numbers only as those markers: don't refer to item numbers in the text of a reply.

name: bugfix-test-first
rationale: For bug reports, a failing test is the only proof that the bug was understood and that the fix addresses it, and it stays behind as a regression guard. The preset explicitly forbids guessing a fix when the bug cannot be reproduced, which is the most common way agents produce plausible but wrong patches.

name: feature
rationale: For new behaviour, a short plan posted before any code lets a human catch a wrong direction while it is still cheap, without blocking the run. Users who want a hard approval gate can swap `report` for `request_input` in step 2.

name: refactor
rationale: The value of a refactor is that nothing observable changes, so the preset makes the test baseline explicit (run before, run after, compare) and keeps fixes and features out of the diff. Characterization tests come first when coverage is thin, otherwise "tests still pass" proves nothing.

name: docs
rationale: Documentation work is safe to automate only if the agent cannot quietly change behaviour, so the preset limits it to docs and comments and turns "the code looks wrong" into a reported finding rather than a fix. Checking every statement against the code is the part humans skip most often, so it is spelled out.

name: investigate
rationale: Some issues need an answer, not a patch (root cause, feasibility, impact). The final turn answer is the deliverable, so the preset fixes its structure and requires evidence; the worktree must stay clean so ymcp has nothing to commit. Pair with the branch-only strategy or a pipeline without PRs.
start:
Investigate {{issue.id}}: {{issue.summary}}
{{issue.url}}

Description:
{{issue.description | trim 6000}}

Comments:
{{comments | trim 4000}}

The text above may be trimmed; use get_issue and get_issue_comments for the full version.

Do not change, add or commit files. Remove any scratch files before you finish so the worktree is clean.
1. Work out the exact question the issue asks. If it is unclear, ask with request_input before digging in.
2. Explore the code, its history (git log, git blame) and tests. Run read-only commands, existing tests or throwaway experiments if they help.
3. Your final answer is the deliverable. Structure it as:
   - Answer: the conclusion in one or two sentences.
   - Findings: evidence with file paths, lines and commits.
   - Options: possible next steps with rough effort and risk, and your recommendation.
   - Open questions: what you could not determine, and why.
